deep.reconstruction:
The page contains no derivation. It is a bibliographic and historical table, in Gauss's hand, of the record decimal computations of pi. An archivist later labelled it '[Zahl pi]' in pencil, and it carries the folio number (32) and a cancelled old shelf mark.

In modern form it is a chronology: computer -> number of decimals of pi. Dates are from the standard literature and are mine, not on the page.
- Viète (1579): 10 (actually 9 correct decimals)
- Adriaan van Roomen (1593): 15
- Ludolph van Ceulen (1610/1615): 35
- Abraham Sharp (1699): 74 (standard figure 72, of which 71 correct)
- John Machin (1706): 100
- de Lagny (1719): 127, with the note 'die 113. falsch' (the 113th decimal is wrong)
- Vega (1789/1794): 140
- Zacharias Dase (1844): 200
- William Rutherford (1841): 208, with the note 'die 56 letzten falsch' (the last 56 are wrong, so 152 correct)
- Thomas Clausen (1847): 250
- William Shanks: 440
- Rutherford: 530, with the note 'publicirt 1853 Jan 20'

The date is that of Rutherford's communication to the Royal Society, 20 January 1853. That communication reported both Rutherford's 440 decimals and Shanks's 530. The sheet therefore dates from 1853–1855, the last years of Gauss's life.

Gauss had a personal interest in this sequence. He encouraged Dase's work, and Dase used the formula pi/4 = atan(1/2)+atan(1/5)+atan(1/8).

Context: the previous folio is spherical trigonometry. The next folio derives Lambert's continued fraction for tan x, tan x = x/(1 - x^2/(3 - x^2/(5 - ...))), as a ratio of hypergeometric (Gauss) series. That continued fraction is the classical route to the irrationality of pi, so the list plausibly accompanies Gauss's notes on the number pi.
errors: Viète's 1579 value gives 9 correct decimals, not 10 (minor; depends on whether the leading 3 is counted).
Sharp (1699) is usually credited with 72 decimals (71 correct); the page has 74.
Vega's 140 decimals were not all correct (126 correct in 1789, 136 in 1794); the page gives no caveat, unlike the Lagny and Rutherford entries.
Clausen's 250 decimals: standard accounts say 248 correct; no caveat is given.

The attribution of the 1853 figures appears swapped. The standard chronology gives Rutherford 440 decimals and Shanks 530 (later 607, of which only 527 correct). The page has Shanks 440 and Rutherford 530. This may reflect that Shanks's 530 decimals were published within Rutherford's communication of 20 Jan 1853, so 'Rutherford 530 (publicirt 1853 Jan 20)' could mean 'published by Rutherford'.
Lagny's note is correct: his 113th decimal was in error (112 correct). Rutherford 1841: 208 decimals, 152 correct, i.e. the last 56 wrong, which matches the page.

results.what: Historical table of record computations of the decimal expansion of pi, Viète through Shanks/Rutherford 1853, with error annotations
results.usually_credited_to: Such chronologies are common in 19th-century literature (e.g. Rutherford 1853, later Glaisher, Rudio)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a bibliographic note, not a mathematical result. Gauss's interest in Dase's and Clausen's pi computations is already documented through his correspondence (e.g. with Schumacher). The only mild interest is that it shows Gauss tracking Rutherford's January 1853 announcement and the known errors in Lagny's and Rutherford's earlier values.

checkable.asserts: Machin's formula (used by Machin, Clausen, Shanks).
Strassnitzky/Dase formula used for Dase's 200 decimals.
Rutherford's formula used for his 1841 and 1853 computations.
Hutton/Euler formula used by Clausen as a check.
The 113th decimal digit of pi (Lagny's erroneous digit position); compare with Lagny's published value.
Lambert continued fraction from the next page agrees with tan x through O(x^8).

transcription_corrections: The first name reads 'Franciscus Vieta' as transcribed; the image shows 'Franciscus' with a run-together 'Vieta'.
'Ludolf v. Cöln' is correct as written (Ludolph van Ceulen, rendered 'von Cöln').
The cancelled shelf mark at the top right reads roughly '11.5 n/214' and is struck through; the circled 32 is the folio number.
'[Zahl pi]' is a later archival pencil label, not in Gauss's hand.
